title: Economics · Episode 2
chapters: Incentives: why rewards so often backfire
Inequality: how the gap between rich and poor is measured

units.t: Economics. Episode two.
In this episode: Incentives: why rewards so often backfire, GDP: measuring an economy and Inequality: how the gap between rich and poor is measured.
Part one. Incentives: why rewards so often backfire.
Offer people a reward and they'll respond, just not always the way you hoped.
Here's why clever incentives can go spectacularly wrong.
The great rat hunt.
In 1902 French colonial authorities in Hanoi faced rats in the city's new sewers, and plague made it urgent.
They offered a small bounty for every rat killed, paid on presentation of a tail.
Soon officials noticed rats running around without tails.
People were cutting off tails for the reward and releasing the rats to breed.
The historian Michael Vann found reports of rat farming too.
The scheme did what it paid for, not what it meant.
People respond to what is actually rewarded, not what the designer intended.
It's one of the most important and most forgotten lessons in economics.
People respond.
If there's one sentence many economists would put on a T shirt, it's 'people respond to incentives'.
An incentive is anything that makes an action more or less attractive: a price, a bonus, a fine, a deadline, even praise or embarrassment.
Raise the price of something and people tend to buy less of it.
Many responses are what policymakers want.
Australia's container deposit schemes and rooftop solar incentives have changed behaviour on a large scale.
The trouble comes when incentives are designed carelessly, because people are quick to find the easiest path to a reward, whether or not it achieves the actual goal.
Measures as targets.
In 1975 the economist Charles Goodhart observed that statistics used to guide policy tend to break down once they become targets.
Marilyn Strathern later summed it up: 'When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.'
A call centre rewarding short call times may find staff hanging up on difficult customers.
A hospital judged on waiting times may find creative ways to reclassify waits.
Schools judged on test scores can end up teaching to the test.
There's an old Soviet era joke about a nail factory: given a target by weight, it made a few giant useless nails; given a target by number, it made millions of tiny ones.
Whatever gets measured gets gamed.
Fines and crowding out.
In a 2000 study, Uri Gneezy and Aldo Rustichini looked at Israeli day care centres where parents were often late.
Some introduced a small fine, and lateness rose.
The paper's title, 'A Fine Is a Price', gives the reason: late pick-up had meant imposing on a teacher's goodwill, but now it felt like a service parents could buy.
When the fines were removed, lateness stayed high.
A cheap financial incentive had replaced a social one, and the old norm didn't return.
Money can crowd out other motives.
In 1970 Richard Titmuss argued that paying for blood could undermine the civic duty of voluntary donors.
Researchers debate how strong this is, and payment raises effort in many settings.
But people are also motivated by pride, fairness and belonging.
Australia's Lifeblood relies on unpaid volunteers.
Moral hazard and design.
Moral hazard is an insurance term: if someone else bears the cost when things go wrong, people may be less careful.
A driver with comprehensive insurance might park carelessly.
A bank expecting a rescue might make riskier loans, keeping profits and passing losses to taxpayers, a worry after 2008.
Insurers use excesses so customers share part of every claim.
It can be managed, not eliminated.
Australia's banking Royal Commission, which reported in 2019, heard many examples of staff chasing commissions and sales targets at customers' expense.
To design better incentives, reward the true goal rather than an easy proxy, imagine how a cynical person might game it and close those loopholes, and use several measures.
Pride, trust and fairness are incentives too.
Ask the rat tail question: what am I really paying for?
The key idea: People respond to what is actually rewarded, not what the designer meant.
Part two. GDP: measuring an economy.
One number gets quoted every quarter as the scorecard for an entire nation.
Here's what it actually counts, and what it quietly leaves out.
What GDP counts.
GDP is the market value of all the final goods and services produced within a country's borders over a set period, usually a quarter or a year.
'Final' matters: a loaf of bread counts, but the baker's flour is not counted again, or it would be double counted.
'Domestic' means inside the country, whoever owns the business.
The Australian Bureau of Statistics publishes GDP every three months.
In the mid-2020s Australia produced roughly $2.
7 trillion a year.

Every dollar spent is someone's output and someone's income, so GDP can be measured three ways: production, value added by industries, income, wages and profits, and expenditure: C + I + G +, X − M. They never match perfectly, so statisticians reconcile them, and revisions are normal.
Real and per person.
If prices rise 4 per cent and output stays flat, the dollar value of GDP still rises about 4 per cent.
That is nominal GDP.
Real GDP adjusts for inflation by valuing output at constant prices, and it is what 'the economy grew 0.
5 per cent last quarter' means.
Australia's real GDP has typically grown around 2 to 3 per cent a year, and 3 per cent growth doubles an economy in roughly 24 years.
A country can also grow GDP simply by adding people.
Australia's population has grown quickly, largely through immigration, so total GDP can rise even when output per person is flat.
That is why economists watch GDP per capita, in the order of $100,000 in the mid-2020s.
In 2023 and 2024 several quarters saw total GDP grow while per person GDP fell, a 'per capita recession'.
What GDP ignores.
GDP only counts activity with a market price.

Cooking dinner at home, raising children, caring for an ageing parent and volunteering with the local fire brigade add nothing, even though the ABS has estimated unpaid work would be worth a very large sum if paid.
Meanwhile some bad events raise GDP.
Rebuilding after a bushfire or flood adds output, but the community is no better off than if the disaster had never happened.
Running down a forest or mineral deposit counts as income, with no deduction for what is used up.
GDP measures activity, not whether that activity is wise.
Beyond GDP.
Modern national accounts grew out of work in the 1930s by economists including Simon Kuznets, who himself warned that a nation's welfare can hardly be inferred from its national income.
In 1968 US senator Robert Kennedy said gross national product, GDP's close cousin, measures everything 'except that which makes life worthwhile'.
GDP ignores leisure, health, pollution, inequality and how safe people feel.
Alternatives include the United Nations' Human Development Index, which adds life expectancy and education, and the OECD's Better Life Index.
In 2023 the Australian Government released 'Measuring What Matters', a framework tracking around 50 indicators of wellbeing alongside traditional economic figures.
Reading the headlines.
Like most rich countries, Australia is mainly a services economy: health care, education, finance, retail, construction and professional services produce most output and employ most workers.
Mining contributes roughly a tenth of GDP in many years and much more of exports, yet employs only around 2 per cent of workers.
Manufacturing has shrunk since the mid-20th century and agriculture is a few per cent of GDP, though both remain important exporters.
Household consumption is around half of GDP.
When figures come out, ask: real or nominal?
Quarterly or annual?
What happened per person?
Which parts drove the change?
One weak quarter is not a crisis, and first estimates are often revised.
Pair GDP with unemployment, wages, inflation and household income.
Some of the most valuable things in your life will never appear in the national accounts.
The key idea: GDP, gross domestic product, is the market value of final goods and services produced in a country over a period, and can be measured by production, income or spending.
Part three. Inequality: how the gap between rich and poor is measured.
Is the gap between rich and poor growing?
The answer depends on what you measure, and economists have been arguing about it for more than a century.
Income versus wealth.
Talk about inequality often blurs two different things.
Income is money that comes in over a period, from wages, business profits, interest, rent or government payments.
Wealth is the stock of what you own minus what you owe: a house, superannuation, shares, savings and a car, less any mortgage or debts.
A young doctor might have a high income but little wealth, while a retired farmer could have modest income and substantial wealth in land.
Across almost every country, wealth is far more unequally distributed than income.
Wealth builds up over a lifetime, earns its own returns and can be passed on, so differences tend to compound over time.
The Gini coefficient.
In 1905 the American economist Max Lorenz proposed a neat way to picture inequality.
Line everyone up from poorest to richest and plot what share of total income the bottom 10 per cent, 20 per cent and so on receive.
If everyone earned the same, the line would be perfectly straight.
The more it sags, the more unequal the society.
In 1912 the Italian statistician Corrado Gini turned this into a single number.
A Gini coefficient of 0 means perfect equality, and 1 means one person has everything.
Most developed countries have income Gini figures between roughly 0.
25 and 0.
40, and wealth figures that are considerably higher.
When averages mislead.
Around 1900, Italian economist Vilfredo Pareto studied tax and property records from several countries and centuries.
He found the top of the distribution followed a similar pattern again and again, with a small share of people holding a large share of the total.
The popular eighty-twenty rule was named after him, though it is far looser than his mathematics.
This power law still describes the top of wealth distributions well.
It means averages can mislead.
If a billionaire walks into a pub, the average wealth soars, yet nobody else is richer.
Economists often prefer the median, the person exactly in the middle, to the mean.
They also compare the 90th and 10th percentiles, or track the top 1 per cent's income share.
Kuznets, Piketty and debate.
In 1955 economist Simon Kuznets suggested that inequality rises as countries industrialise and then falls as they mature, an upside-down U called the Kuznets curve.
The mid-twentieth century seemed to prove him right, as gaps narrowed in many rich countries.
Then, from around 1980, top income shares rose again in the United States, Britain and elsewhere.
In 2013 French economist Thomas Piketty published Capital in the Twenty-First Century, arguing that when the return on capital exceeds the growth rate of the economy, wealth tends to concentrate.
His book became a surprise bestseller and drew strong criticism, with economists still debating his data, his theory and his proposed wealth taxes.
Can you climb the ladder.
A snapshot of inequality does not say whether the same people stay at the top or bottom.
Economic mobility asks how strongly your adult income is linked to your parents' income.
Research led by economist Miles Corak found that countries with higher inequality tend to have lower mobility between generations, a link dubbed the Great Gatsby curve by Alan Krueger in 2012.
It is a correlation, and researchers debate what drives it, from education and housing to social networks.
Measured mobility in Australia has generally been found to be higher than in the United States, though comparing countries is tricky.
Many people care less about the gap itself than about whether the ladder is climbable.
The key idea: Income is what flows in each year; wealth is what you own, and it is usually far more unequal.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What went wrong with the Hanoi rat bounty?
Answer. People bred rats and cut off tails for cash.
Question two. Why isn't the flour a baker buys counted separately in GDP?
Answer. Its value is already in the bread.
Question three. Why is wealth usually more unequal than income?
Answer. It compounds and can be inherited.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
